lesson.title: Mir ist kalt: Dative Feelings
lesson.subtitle: Dative-experiencer expressions — five drills for cold, bored, and sorry

hook.title: Feelings Happen To You
hook.content: English says I AM cold. German says it is cold TO ME: Mir ist kalt. I am bored? — Mir ist langweilig (to-me it is boring). I am sorry? — Es tut mir leid (it does me sorrow). The pattern is ancient: the experiencer is a receiver, not an actor — feelings arrive, they are not performed. English used to agree: methinks, 'me seems', 'it grieves me'. German kept the whole grammar of being-affected: mir, dir, ihm — and twelve expressions you will use every week.

footnotes.title: The Weather Is Also Dative
footnotes.content: Notice what is really cold: ES ist kalt — 'it', the impersonal subject. The German sentence has no 'I' as subject at all: Es (the situation) ist (is) mir (to-me) kalt (cold). You are not the cold thing; you are the one the cold happens to. Exactly like methinks: it thinks itself to me.

pattern.title: The Feeling Fridge
pattern.content: Temperature: Mir ist kalt / warm / heiß (to-me it is cold/warm/hot). States: Mir ist langweilig (bored), Mir ist schlecht (I feel sick), Mir ist schwindlig (dizzy); for well-being say 'es geht mir gut'. Sorrow: Es tut mir leid (it does me sorrow — I am sorry). Recipient: Das tut mir weh (that does me pain — that hurts). Grammar recipe: [Es] + ist/tut + [dative pronoun] + [the feeling]. Swap mir for dir/ihm and you can diagnose anyone: Ist dir kalt? (are YOU cold — to-thee?).
pattern.linguist_note: These are the same dative-experiencer constructions English kept only in fossils ('me seems', 'it grieves me to say'). German's everyday emotional vocabulary is grammatically archaic English — and fully alive.

exercises.prompt: The feeling fridge — match each expression with its literal reading:

matching_pairs.english: It is cold to me (I'm cold)
It is boring to me (I'm bored)
It is unwell to me (I feel sick)

exercises.target_answer: Mir ist kalt, Mir ist langweilig, Es tut mir leid, Das tut mir weh, Mir ist übel
exercises.meaning: it is cold to me, it is boring to me, it does me sorrow, it does me pain, I feel sick
exercises.explanation: Feelings arrive at the dative — you are the receiver, never the performer. übel is the oldest of the lot: evil, unwell.

exercises.prompt: Diagnose a friend: 'Ist _____ kalt?' (Are YOU cold — to-thee?):
exercises.meaning: Ist dir kalt? = Are you cold (is it cold to-thee)?
exercises.explanation: The experiencer dative swaps with the person: mir → dir → ihm. dich would make you the object — nobody 'coldens' you. The dative judges state: mir ist schlecht, mir ist lustig — Bist du fertig? stays sein's.

exercises.prompt: 'Es tut mir leid' — which ancient verb hides in 'tut'?
exercises.meaning: tun ↔ do: the oldest verb twin
exercises.explanation: The apology is an English sentence: 'it does me sorrow'. The do-support English invented — this is the same verb.

exercises.prompt: Swap the experiencer: 'Mir ist kalt' for him (TO HIM it is cold):
exercises.meaning: Ihm ist kalt = He is cold (to-him it is cold)
exercises.explanation: Ihm — the dative of er, the twin of English 'give it him'. Feelings transfer person to person with one word. Der Mensch is the experiencer, die Leute the crowd, der Himmel the sky — the whole dative cast.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I am sorry, but it is boring'
exercises.target_answer: Es tut mir leid aber es ist langweilig
exercises.meaning: I am sorry, but it is boring

vocab_hints.note: am Meer — the place the wind comes from, and the place the Urlaub goes: Am Meer ist mir kalt, im Urlaub ist mir gut.

exercises.explanation: Two experiencer frames in one sentence — tut mir leid (it does me sorrow) and ist langweilig (it is boring to-me, mir implied). Add the place and the same frame covers the coast: Am Meer ist mir kalt — at the sea it is cold to me; im Urlaub ist mir gut — on holiday it goes well for me.

summary.outcome: Use the dative-experiencer expressions for cold, bored, sorry, and hurt.

use_example.german: Es tut mir leid, aber mir ist kalt.

summary.takeaway: Feelings happen TO you: mir ist kalt/langweilig, es tut mir leid — the methinks grammar, alive and daily.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the Capstone sprigs — the full Berlin reading with tap-to-inspect words and the whole-trail review game.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "Today that is very good"
twist.explanation: Building "Heute ist das sehr gut" from the lesson's core pattern locks in Mir ist kalt: Dative Feelings.

mir.context_translation: Can you please help me? (literally: help to me)
mir.etymology_derivation: Dative of ich — the same ancient pronoun as English me, keeping the 'to me' meaning (mir ist kalt = it is cold to me). [wiktionary]

dir.etymology_derivation: Dative of du — the exact twin of archaic English 'I give it thee'; the dative is the giving case. [wiktionary]

ihm.etymology_derivation: Dative of er — the exact twin of English him; the h dropped from speech and stayed in spelling. [wiktionary]

tun.context_translation: I am sorry (literally: it does sorrow to me).

übel.context_translation: I feel a bit sick today.
übel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *ubil — English evil is the documented cognate; both descend from the same ancient word for bad. [wiktionary]

schlecht.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *slihtaz 'smooth, level' — Wiktionary: cognate with English slight. [wiktionary]

fertig.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fartig, literally journey-ready, from fart (journey), the ancestor of modern Fahrt; the root belongs with the Germanic travel word behind English fare, and Dutch has the parallel vaardig. [wiktionary]

lustig.etymology_derivation: Lust (desire, joy) plus -ig; Lust is the exact cognate of English lust, from Proto-Germanic *lustuz, though in German the sexual shade is weak and the word still means plain pleasure, as in Lust haben. [wiktionary]

langweilig.etymology_derivation: Langeweile (long while) + -ig — literally 'long-while-ish'; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

leute.context_translation: Many people are waiting at the station.
leute.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *liudiz, kin to the Old English leode (men, people); German keeps the plural-only collective with the standard article die Leute. [wiktionary]

himmel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *himil — the same Germanic line as English heaven's root family. [wiktionary]

mensch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *manniskaz 'human', built on Mann — English mannish is the cognate form. [wiktionary]

meer.etymology_derivation: From Old High German meri, from Proto-West Germanic *mari. English mere is the listed cognate, and Latin mare is cognate through Indo-European. [wiktionary]

urlaub.context_phrase: Ich fahre im Urlaub nach Italien.
urlaub.context_translation: I go to Italy on vacation.
urlaub.etymology_derivation: Middle High German urloup 'permission to be away', kin to erlauben — cognate with English leave. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
